en: *Inquiry on the Pure Land*:
Compiled by the Master Linji Tianru Ze of the Yuan Dynasty;
annotated by Yunqi Zhuhong.
While his disciple Guangxin was proofreading [the texts], the elder Tianru was sitting in quiet contemplation within the Woyun (Clouds Amidst Mountains) chamber.
A guest pushed open the door and entered;
it was the Zen master Shangren.
He invited him to sit.
After sitting for a long time, the setting sun was shining through the window and the incense smoke was about to fade.
The guest then adjusted his robes, rose,
and asked with composed grace:
"I have heard that Master Yongmingyou received the teaching of the single transmission from National Teacher Tiantai Shaokang."
He was a grandson of Fayuan.
He guided his disciples at Jingci Temple in Hangzhou,
where those under his tutelage always numbered in the thousands.
His quick-witted eloquence and intellectual brilliance were as swift as thunder and wind;
throughout the land, the monastic communities esteemed him as a great master.
Yet, apart from his discourse on Chan, [he was also proficient in other matters].

He personally cultivated the practices for the Pure Land and further instructed others in them, composing works such as the *Jian shi xi fang deng wen* (Text on Selecting and Showing the Western [Pure Land]*) which were widely disseminated throughout the world. *(Note: The title provided in the source text appears to be a reconstruction; the most famous work by this author related to this theme is the *Jian shi xi fang jing tu yi lun* (Treatise on Selecting and Showing the Western Pure Land).)*
He also composed a verse of fourfold discernment,
which says in brief:
"There may be Chan without Pure Land."
Nine out of ten go astray;
without meditation, there is the Pure Land.
Of ten thousand who practice, ten thousand depart.
Observing such statements of his as he advocates for the Pure Land—
standing as steeply as ten-thousand-fathom cliffs without the slightest concession—
is it not that he has instead compromised his own Chan practice while excessively praising the Pure Land?
"This doubt is no small matter;
Master, please explain it for me.
He replied:
How great is this question!
You should know that Yongming’s praise was no exaggeration;
he rendered profound service to the teachings and the tradition.
It is regrettable that Yongming merely set forth its general outline without fully elucidating it;
consequently, he was unable to completely dispel the doubts of practitioners of Chan.
I am but a humble student of Chan and have not yet mastered the teachings on the Pure Land;
nevertheless, I have also perused various texts concerning the Pure Land.
I have gained a slight general understanding of it.
Fundamentally, this is a method that is easy to practice and easy to enter,
yet it is also a teaching that is difficult to explain and difficult to believe.
Therefore, when Śākyamuni, our compassionate Father, was present in the world,
he preached the Amitābha Sūtra for his disciples,
knowing in advance that sentient beings during the Dharma-ending age would rarely be able to believe and turn toward it with devotion.
Therefore, he cites the Buddhas of the six directions extending their broad and long tongues to speak words of truth,
thereby giving rise to faith and destroying doubt.
And at the end of the sutra,
because of the praise bestowed by all the Buddhas,
he further speaks for himself:
You should know that I perform this difficult task in the world of the five turbidities;
for the sake of all the worlds, I preach this Dharma which is difficult to believe—
this is truly most difficult.
All of these are bitter words of earnest exhortation intended to encourage people toward faith and devotion.
Furthermore, as the Great Compassionate World-Honored One has descended to save the final age,
whatever has been proclaimed from his golden mouth—
While no one— whether human or non-human— fails to believe in, accept, and practice even a single verse or a single line [of the scriptures],
why is it that regarding the teaching of the Pure Land alone,
there are still those who harbor doubts?
This is truly because the teaching of the Pure Land is most vast and great,
while the practice of the Pure Land is most concise and easy;
it is precisely because it is both vast and great, yet concise and easy, that [it is so effective].
Those who hear this cannot help but harbor doubts.
That which is called "vast and great" encompasses and gathers all capacities and faculties without exception.
Above, even Bodhisattvas in their final birth before enlightenment at the stage of Equal Enlightenment are born in the Pure Land;
below, even the ignorant masses—fools and women alike—and those who have committed the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds, being devoid of wisdom, are likewise born there.
If, at the time of death, one is able to recite the Buddha’s name, repent of one's transgressions,
and direct one’s heart toward the Pure Land,
all such persons shall attain rebirth there.
What is called "simplicity" means that,
from the outset, there are no practices involving hardship or toil,
nor are there any conditions for confusion or differentiation.
Simply by upholding the four-character name of Amitābha Buddha,
one thereby attains liberation from Saṃsāra and achieves rebirth in Sukhāvatī.
One attains non-retrogression,
continuing until the attainment of Buddhahood, after which it ceases.
Since its vastness is such as that, [it is immeasurable].
Its simplicity is such as this;
therefore, even the wise cannot help but harbor doubts about it.
If you understand this, [you will be free from doubt].
Thus, we know that Yongming’s praise was profoundly intentional and not excessive.
A questioner asked:
"I have already heard your instructions regarding its vastness and simplicity."
As for those in the Chan school who have attained enlightenment,
since it is said that "seeing one's nature is to become a Buddha," would they ever be willing to seek rebirth in a Pure Land?
The answer is:
It is simply that you do not yet understand.
Those who have attained awakening and realization truly desire to seek birth [in the Pure Land].
An ancient said:
"If one is not born in the Pure Land,
what other land could one be born in?"
You have merely not yet awakened.
Once you have awakened,
then your course toward the Pure Land will be such that ten thousand oxen could not pull you back.
Question: The Buddhas and patriarchs appear in the world to deliver sentient beings;
yet students suffer only from their failure to clarify the Great Matter.
The Great Matter having been clarified,
one should practice the Buddha’s teachings,
manifesting transformation bodies according to the various types of beings.
Entering the mud and entering the water, they do not avoid birth and death to extensively deliver sentient beings;
such are those of the present who have attained awakening.
To seek birth in the Pure Land is to loathe suffering and pursue happiness,
regardless of others.
"This is not what I desire.
He replied,
"It is like seeing an egg and seeking the rooster."
Why such premature reckoning?
Do you suppose that after a single awakening, habitual outflows are forever eliminated and one immediately attains non-retrogression?
Do you suppose that after a single awakening, there are no further matters of universally studying the Buddha-dharma, practicing, or realizing the fruits?
Do you suppose that after a single awakening one can immediately equal the Buddhas, entering birth and death without being disturbed by the hindrances of conditions?
If this is truly so, [then it is as you say].
Then, as for the great Bodhisattvas who cultivate the six perfections and the myriad practices for as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges—
would they not surely feel ashamed before you?
The ancient teachings state:
"Even Śrāvakas still possess the delusion of emerging from the womb;
even Bodhisattvas likewise experience the darkness of being separated from their deceased parents."
How much more so for those of recent times who possess but a meager understanding and shallow realization, unable even to save themselves?
Even among those who have attained profound insights and possess lofty perspectives,
whose practice and understanding correspond with one another and whose resolve is set on liberating others— how many are there?
Alas, how can one who has not yet ascended to the stage of non-retrogression,
whose power and function are not yet sufficient,
dwell within this defiled and evil world to transform those who are so stubborn and fierce?
This, too, was not permitted by the former sages;
it is like attempting to ferry many people across a treacherous sea with a boat that is incomplete and unstable—
wherein both self and others will drown together.
This principle is necessarily so.
Therefore, the *Wangsheng lun* (Treatise on Rebirth) says:
"Those who wish to sport at the gates of hell..."
Having necessarily been born in that land and attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*),
one returns to the realm of birth and death to rescue suffering sentient beings;
for these reasons, one seeks birth in the Pure Land.
Furthermore, a former sage said:
"Until one has attained the stage of non-retrogression,
it is not possible to mingle with worldly society while saving sentient beings."
Until one attains the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti),
one must never be separated from the Buddha,
just as an infant is never separated from its mother.
Furthermore, it is like a fledgling with weak wings that can only cling to a branch.
Now, within this land, Śākyamuni has already passed away and Maitreya has not yet been born;
how much more so when one is entangled by the causes and effects of suffering in the four evil destinies?
Heterodox teachers and malevolent spirits sow discord with their partisan provocations;
the signs of beautiful forms and lewd sounds cause delusion;
and foul conditions and defiling contacts encroach upon one another.
Since there is no manifest Buddha upon whom to rely,
and one is further disturbed by external conditions,
those who have attained awakening at the initial stage of the mind...
There are few who do not encounter such decline and defeat;
for this reason, there is indeed a profound significance in the World-Honored One’s earnest exhortation to take rebirth in Sukhāvatī.
For Amitābha currently preaches the Dharma there;
the conditions and environment of that Land of Bliss are variously pure.
If one relies upon that Buddha, the power of patience will be easily accomplished.
Having personally attained the high stage of Buddhahood and received a direct prophecy,
he subsequently emerged to transform sentient beings.
There is no obstruction regarding the past and the future. For this reason,
even those of superior faculties and sharp instruments [of wisdom].
If even they still wish to take rebirth,
how much more so for those of you of middling or inferior capacity who have only recently attained enlightenment?
Have you not seen this?
In the *Buddhanusmṛtisamādhisūtra*,
Mañjuśrī himself recounts his past causes,
stating that by attaining the buddhānusmṛti-samādhi, he is constantly reborn in the pure lands.
The World-Honored One further prophesied of him, saying:
"You shall be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Furthermore, he was not seen again.
In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*,
Samantabhadra exhorted the youth Sudhana and the great assembly at the oceanic gathering to take the ten great vows as their guide for returning to the Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī).
The verse says: "May I,
when the time approaches for my life to end,
completely eliminate all obstacles."
One will behold that Buddha Amitābha face-to-face and immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
It further says:
The assembly of that Buddha was entirely pure;
at that time, I was born from a supreme lotus and personally beheld the Tathāgata of Immeasurable Light.
He bestowed upon me the prophecy of my future enlightenment.
Having received that prophecy from the Tathāgata,
I manifested countless hundreds of koṭis of emanation bodies.
The power of their wisdom is vast, pervading the ten directions,
bringing benefit and happiness to the entire realm of sentient beings;
yet they are not seen.
In the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*,
the verse concerning the prophecy for Nāgārjuna states:
"In the land of South India..."
There was a bhikṣu of great name and virtue,
whose title was Nāgārjuna;
he was able to shatter the tenets of existence and non-existence.
He shall manifest my unsurpassed Mahāyāna Dharma within the world,
attain the first stage of Joy,
and be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
Furthermore, it is not seen that the Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa has [such a statement] in the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.
The aspiration to seek birth [in the Pure Land].
In the *Treatise on Infinite Life* (*Wúliàngshòu lùn*),
the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu possessed the heart that aspires to go there.
Furthermore, it is not seen that in the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra*,
Śuddhodana Rāja and seventy thousand members of the Śākya clan were granted permission to be born together in Sukhāvatī.
In the *Sūtra of the Sixteen Contemplations*,
it is indicated that Lady Vaidehī and her five hundred attendants shall together behold Amitābha;
such is the case for those such as Śuddhodana and Vaidehī.
All of them have currently attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Among those of this kind in Western India, they are beyond counting.
In the Eastern Land, there were those such as Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu who gathered a society of eminent practitioners;
and the venerable masters of various schools, such as Tiantai and Xianshou, who cultivated themselves and transformed others—
whether monastics or laypeople— all of whom were born together in the Pure Land.
Furthermore, can they even be numbered? Consider,
for instance, the great Bodhisattvas Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra,
and the multitude of Sudhana’s spiritual friends whom he visited throughout the ocean-like assembly.
His awakening was equal to that of the various sages.
Aśvaghoṣa, Nāgārjuna, and others were also bodhisattvas;
they are likewise regarded by the Chan school as great ancestral masters.
Compared to those sages who have realized and attained this,
how do those of the present day who claim to have attained realization measure up?
They still aspire to be born in a land of bliss and draw near to Amitābha;
yet you, after a single awakening—
If you no longer seek birth [in the realms of existence],
how can Nāgārjuna, Aśvaghoṣa, Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī,
and the others not feel shame before you?
Now, why do you not examine your own mind and measure your own strength?
Is that which you have cultivated and realized truly superior to that of the two Bodhisattvas and the two Chan patriarchs?
The spiritual friends you have consulted and the Buddha-nature you have realized—
surely these surpass even the ocean-like assembly of Sudhana?
You have attained the patient acceptance of the dharma of non-self-nature and received the seal of certification from the Buddhas.
Could there truly be anyone who surpasses Śuddhodana and Vaidehī?
King Śuddhodana was the father of the Buddha,
and the seventy thousand members of the Śākya clan were his kinsmen.
If birth in the Pure Land were of no benefit,
would the Buddha have endured the suffering of his father and kinsmen?
It was previously said that those who have attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas may be permitted to mingle with the mundane world to save sentient beings.
Now, since even your father, the King, and his kinsmen have attained this patience (kṣānti) yet still maintain the memory of their future rebirths,
how much more so should you harbor the intention to seek their protection and care.
Is this not indeed profound and far-reaching?
I have often observed that those who practice Chan today fail to investigate the definitive meaning of the Tathāgata.
Failing to understand the profound mystery of Bodhidharma’s teaching,
they remain empty-minded and arrogant, habitually indulging in such madness that upon seeing others practice Pure Land Buddhism, they mock them, saying:
He emulates the conduct of ignorant men and women;
how vulgar this is!
I have often discussed this matter.
It is not that these are base, ignorant men or women;
rather, it is that [the teachings of] Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, Nāgārjuna, Aśvaghoṣa, and others are base.
It is not merely that they themselves are deluded regarding the Right Path.
They lose their own roots of goodness;
they destroy their own body of wisdom;
they extinguish their own lineage of the Buddha.
Furthermore, one will incur the karma of slandering the Dharma and invite the calamity of disparaging the Sages;
the Buddhas and Patriarchs regard such a person as one to be pitied.
Thereupon, Master Yongming felt deep compassion and piteous sorrow for him;
he exposed his heart and liver to advocate for the Pure Land,
having already cultivated it himself.
Furthermore, because he transforms the world,
at the time of his passing he knows in advance that the moment has arrived;
thereupon, various kinds of extraordinary and sublime signs appear.
Even his body was encrusted with scales like those of a śāli fish.
Once, there was a monk from Fuzhou who circumambulated his stupa for many years.
When people asked him the reason for this,
the monk said,
"Because of my illness, I entered the realm of the dead."
Because his lifespan in the realm of the living had not yet ended, King Yama permitted him to be released and returned to life; thereupon,
he saw [the following] to the left of the hall.
He made offerings to a single hanging scroll of a monk, and King Yama paid his respects with great earnestness.
He then questioned the presiding official, who said:
This is Chan Master Yongming Shou.
Through his diligent cultivation,
he was reborn directly in the highest grade of the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
The King, considering this a rare occurrence,
had his likeness painted and paid him reverent homage. Indeed,
during the Yongming era, he had already awakened to the Chan of direct pointing taught by Bodhidharma.
Furthermore, it can lead one’s body to the highest grade of rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
By means of this, the misconceptions of those who practice meditation are resolved;
by means of this, those living in the Dharma-ending age are encouraged to have faith.
Therefore, I maintain that he has rendered profound service to our religious tradition;
this is not true only of Yongming,
but also of Chan Master Sixin Xin, for instance.
In a text composed to encourage the cultivation of the Pure Land, it is said:
"Amitābha is very easy to recite;
the Pure Land is very easy to be born in."
It is further said:
"For those who practice Chan meditation, it is best to recite the Buddha's name.
Their spiritual faculties may be dull."
"Fearing that I may not attain great awakening in this life,
I shall instead rely on the power of Amitābha’s vows to be guided to rebirth in the Pure Land.
It further says:
"If you do not attain birth in the Pure Land through mindfulness of the Buddha, this old monk shall fall into the Hell of the Torn-out Tongue.
Furthermore, Zen Master Zhenxie Le said in his discourse on the Pure Land: "It is said..."
The entire tradition of the Caodong school is dedicated to esoteric cultivation.
What is the reason for this?
It is truly because the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation is a direct path for practice.
Directly following the Great Canon to engage those of the highest faculties,
while indirectly citing other sources to guide those of middling and lower capacities.
Furthermore, it is said:
"The great masters of the Zen school have already realized the Dharma that is neither empty nor existent;
yet they maintain their resolve with diligent devotion to the practice of purity."
Is it not the case that for those who have attained the vision of the Buddha through non-pure karma, the approach of the Chan school is more accessible?
Furthermore, it is said:
"Whether it be Buddhas or Patriarchs, whether in the Exoteric Teachings or in Chan."
All cultivate pure karma and return together to a single source.
Once one enters this gate,
one is able to enter all immeasurable dharma-gates.
As for such masters as Chan Master Tianyi Huai,
Chan Master Yuanzhao Ben,
and Chan Master Cishou Shen.
Chan Master Si of Nanyue,
Chan Master Fazhao,
and Chan Master Jing’ai.
Chan Master Datong of Jingci;
Chan Master Huaiyu of Tiantai;
and Chan Master Daozhen of the Liang Dynasty.
Chan Master Daochuo of the Tang dynasty;
Chan Master Fazhen of Pilin;
and Chan Master Shoun of Gusu.
The Chan Master Beijian Jian,
the Chan Master Tianmu Li, and other such great elders were all master craftsmen of the Chan school.
When one investigates their secret cultivation and manifest teachings,
they are in agreement without being explicitly constrained, in their exaltation of the principles of the Pure Land.
Is this not true not only for the various great elders?
I have once heard an old master say:
"If one were to synthesize the lineages of the five houses..."
Among all the Chan monks in the world,
whether they have attained enlightenment or not,
there is not a single one who does not return to the Pure Land.
When asked the reason for this,
he replied:
"It is like the Chan Master Baizhang Dazhihai."
He was the successor who transmitted the Way of Mazu of Jiangxi;
the monastic communities throughout the world were established in reliance upon him from ancient times until the present.
Not a single person dared to discuss his errors;
the world’s pure regulations were implemented according to his example from beginning to end.
Not a single matter dares to contravene his regulations.
Observe the rules for reciting for sick monks as he describes them:
"The assembly gathers and raises a single verse in unison."
Praise Amitābha Buddha. Then,
together with others, recite "Namo Amitābha Buddha" in unison,
whether a hundred times or a thousand times.
The prayer for dedication reads:
May all conditions that remain be exhausted,
and may you swiftly attain ease and tranquility.
The great mandate is difficult to evade;
he returns directly to An-yang.
Is this not the ultimate destination of the Pure Land?
Furthermore, observe how he escorts deceased monks.
During the recitations at nightfall, he offers this dedication, praying:
"May their spirits transcend to the pure realm."
Karmic toil having ceased,
the lotus of the highest grade blossomed;
the Buddha bestowed upon him the prediction of his final birth.
Is this not the ultimate destination of the Pure Land?
As for the occasion of cremation,
there is nothing else to be done.
Simply have the *vinaya-dhara* lead by chanting aloud, "Namo Amitābha Buddha of the Western World of Ultimate Bliss,
Greatly Compassionate and Benevolent," and as he chants this ten times, the assembly responds in unison ten times.
These are collectively termed the "Ten Recitations.
Having finished chanting, one again performs the dedication, saying:
"The ten recitations chanted above serve as an aid for rebirth in the Pure Land."
Is this not the ultimate destination of the Pure Land?
Since the time of Baizhang,
this has been the means by which Chan monks are sent off.
All rely upon this Dharma.
Thus, what is called the unification of the five lineages encompasses all Zen monks throughout the world.
"There is not a single person who does not return to the Pure Land; how could this not be so?
From my observation of the words cited by the venerable elder,"
This indeed has its basis and cannot be disputed. Furthermore, through his words,
I have come to realize the intent behind the founding patriarch Baizhang’s establishment of the monastic rules.
Furthermore, how could this be so without some basis?
You have escorted Chan monks through the monastic forests countless times;
you surely know this well.
These dedications of the ten recitations were chanted from the mouth and heard by the ears.
Furthermore, I do not know how many more times this will happen.
Since you have neither grasped the meaning of the Patriarch’s intent nor aroused the mind of self-reflection and awakening, [you will continue to suffer].
To falsely claim that those who have attained awakening do not wish for rebirth [in the Pure Land] is a view held by no one else among the world’s Chan practitioners as you are.
Someone asked:
The Pure Land’s gathering of sentient beings is indeed vast beyond measure;
I, a fool, dare not further debate this matter.
Nevertheless, I have also heard the teaching that there is a "Pure Land of Mind-Only" and an "Amitābha of Original Nature."
I, a fool, have privately rejoiced in this.
Yet, upon examining the sūtras and śāstras on the Pure Land,
that which is called the "Pure Land" is as follows:
The Land of Ultimate Bliss lies beyond hundreds of thousands of billions of lands.
That which is called Amitābha is the presiding teacher within that Land of Ultimate Bliss;
thus, he and I are entirely distinct.
"It lies far beyond the fundamental nature of mind-only.
What, then, does this mean?
He replied:
Your statement is narrow-minded;
you do not recognize the vastness, clarity, and subtlety of your own mind.
As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
From the physical body outward, including the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth—
all are objects within the wondrously luminous true mind.
It further says:
All phenomena that arise are manifested solely by the mind.
How could there be a Buddha-land that does not reside within my own mind?
One should know that the Pure Land is nothing but the mind.
There is no land outside the mind,
just as when a great ocean manifests a multitude of bubbles;
not a single bubble can exist apart from the sea.
The Pure Land is solely mind;
outside of the land, there is no mind,
just as all dust relies upon the great earth.
There is not a single speck of dust that is not called "ground.
Furthermore, one should know that the former sages have said:
"This single mind alone possesses the four kinds of lands."
The first is called the Land of Common Abode for Ordinary Beings and Sages;
the second is called the Land of Residual Existence through Expedient Means;
the third is called the Land of True Reward Free from Obstruction.
The fourth is the Land of Constant Quiescent Light.
First, regarding the Land of Common Abode for Ordinary Beings and Sages,
it itself is divided into two categories.
The first is called the defiled land of cohabitation;
the second is called the pure land of cohabitation.
Regarding the first, the defiled land of cohabitation:
The inhabitants of this Sahā world are such as these.
Among those who dwell therein are both ordinary beings and sages;
furthermore, there are two categories for each of these—ordinary and sage.
Generally, there are two types of beings:
first, evil beings, which refers to those in the four realms of existence;
second, virtuous beings, which refers to humans and devas.
There are two kinds of noble abodes:
first, the actual noble ones,
which are the four fruits [of the path].
The Pratyekabuddha corresponds to the sixth stage of the Shared Teaching and the tenth abode of the Distinct Teaching.
Upon completing the final mind of the ten stages of faith,
although pervasive delusions are exhausted,
the retribution body still remains.
All are termed "real.
Second are the "expedient sages," referring to Dharma-body bodhisattvas and Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas within the lands of Expediency, True Reward, and Peaceful Light.
To benefit those with whom he has a karmic connection,
he should manifest birth in their same realm;
all such acts are expedient means.
Because these beings dwell together with ordinary worldlings,
it is called "Ordinary Beings and Sages Dwelling Together.
They also dwell together with those in the four realms of existence.
Therefore, it is called a defiled land (*saṃkliṣṭa-bhūmi*).
Next, regarding the shared pure land (*sādhāraṇa-śuddha-bhūmi*):
take, for example, the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī-kṣetra*).
Although its retributive fruit is so preeminent that it cannot be compared to anything else,
it is nonetheless a place where ordinary beings and sages dwell together. Why is this?
Although there are no four realms of rebirth,
there are humans and devas;
for those born in that land are not necessarily all individuals who have attained the Way.
As a sutra states:
"Those who have committed grave offenses may,
at the time of death, repent and recite the Buddha's name."
One immediately attains rebirth therein. Thus,
it is known that even though one possesses afflictions and defilements,
one may still dwell there.
The noble abodes (āryāvāsa) may be understood as being similar to the preceding [pure abodes] in terms of their provisional and ultimate aspects;
they are called "pure" simply because the four evil destinies are absent there.
Alternatively, it is said:
The characteristics of the Pure Land are fully manifest,
yet they are largely different from others,
such as the Akaniṣṭha realm.
Although it is a pure land,
it still contains men and women as well as Mount Sumeru and other such features;
since pure lands differ from one another in this way, [the question arises].
The defiled lands (saṃkliṣṭa-kṣetra) should likewise be unequal.
Second, the land of skillful means with remainder (upāya-śeṣa-bhūmi) is the dwelling place of those of the two vehicles and of bodhisattvas who have realized the path of skillful means (upāyamārga).
Why is this? If one cultivates the two contemplations and exhausts all pervasive delusions,
yet the distinct delusions as numerous as motes of dust and ignorance remain unsevered,
one abandons the body of分段 (fen-duan, *bheda-deha*).
They are born outside the realm of birth-and-death and receive the Dharma-nature body;
yet they still possess transformation and change.
The land where they dwell is named "Having Remainder" because ignorance has not been severed;
it is named "Expedient Means."
It is the dwelling place of those who practice through skillful means.
Therefore, the *Śāstra* says:
"Beyond the three realms, there is a Pure Land."
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are born therein;
they receive the dharma-nature body,
which is not a birth through the division of segments.
Third, as for the land of true recompense free from obstacles:
it is devoid of those of the two vehicles and is inhabited exclusively by Bodhisattvas of the Dharma-body.
Although one has shattered the obscuring dharmatā and attained the fruit of reality,
ignorance is not yet exhausted.
Moistened by untainted karma,
one receives the Dharmatā-sambhogakāya,
which is also called the Fruition-Reward Land (Phala-vipāka-kṣetra).
